title: Seeing Inside Without Cutting
endLine: X-ray scans see hidden air and water without slicing specimens open.

scenes.tts: How do you see inside a living stem or insect without cutting it open? Hidden tubes carry water in plants and air in insects. Cutting can change what you want to measure. X-rays look inside without a cut.
scenes.caption: How do you see inside a living stem or insect without cutting it open? Hidden tubes carry water in plants and air in insects. Cutting can change what you want to measure. X-rays look inside without a cut.
scenes.visual: Schematic X-ray imaging stage carried through the whole film: an X-ray source on the left, a rotating specimen holder in the centre filling most of the frame height, and a reconstruction window on the right. An opaque intact plant stem stands on the holder with a large question mark over its middle; a faint X-ray beam sweeps through it intact.
scenes.narration: How do you see inside a living stem or insect without cutting it open? Hidden tubes carry water in plants and air in insects. Cutting can change what you want to measure. X-rays look inside without a cut.

scenes.visual: Title 'Seeing Inside Without Cutting' appears cleanly in high-contrast text above the imaging stage while the X-ray beam warms up with slow ambient motion (schematic).

scenes.tts: In X-ray microtomography, or micro C T, an intact stem is imaged from many angles. The images combine into one three-dimensional picture. Air-filled and water-filled xylem conduits, the water tubes, look different in that scan. You can spot an embolism, a gas bubble blocking a conduit, without cutting.
scenes.caption: In X-ray microtomography, or microCT, an intact stem is imaged from many angles. The images combine into one three-dimensional picture. Air-filled and water-filled xylem conduits, the water tubes, look different in that scan. You can spot an embolism, a gas bubble blocking a conduit, without cutting.
scenes.visual: Same imaging stage (schematic): the intact stem rotates steadily on the central holder as the X-ray beam passes through from left to right. On the right window, angle-by-angle projections combine into a 3D cross-section of vertical xylem conduits, blue for water-filled and pale gaps for air-filled embolisms, with one bubble highlighted as 'Embolism'.
scenes.narration: In X-ray microtomography, or microCT, an intact stem is imaged from many angles. The images combine into one three-dimensional picture. Air-filled and water-filled xylem conduits, the water tubes, look different in that scan. You can spot an embolism, a gas bubble blocking a conduit, without cutting.

scenes.tts: What if the inside is moving? A synchrotron, a particle accelerator making very bright X-rays, can film small living animals. On the same stage, it films an insect's air tubes, called tracheae, moving.
scenes.caption: What if the inside is moving? A synchrotron, a particle accelerator making very bright X-rays, can film small living animals. On the same stage, it films an insect's air tubes, called tracheae, moving.
scenes.visual: Same stage (schematic): the left source intensifies and takes the label 'Synchrotron beam'. The stem morphs into a live beetle on the central holder; the right window shifts from static 3D slice to moving X-ray footage showing internal branching tubes labelled 'Tracheae' compressing and expanding rhythmically.
scenes.narration: What if the inside is moving? A synchrotron, a particle accelerator making very bright X-rays, can film small living animals. On the same stage, it films an insect's air tubes, called tracheae, moving.

scenes.tts: Scan an intact stem whose xylem conduits are full of water. That water is pulled up as a column; drought raises the pull, called tension. Cut the stem under water while under tension, and scan again. Several conduits now hold air. Already there, or made by the cut?
scenes.caption: Scan an intact stem whose xylem conduits are full of water. That water is pulled up as a column; drought raises the pull, called tension. Cut the stem under water while under tension, and scan again. Several conduits now hold air. Already there, or made by the cut?
scenes.visual: Same stage (schematic): the intact plant stem returns to the holder. The right window shows a 'Before cut' slice with all conduits blue and water-filled. A blade cuts the stem under water on the stage while upward tension arrows fade, and an 'After cut' slice appears beside it with several pale air-filled conduits and a question mark.
scenes.narration: Scan an intact stem whose xylem conduits are full of water. That water is pulled up as a column; drought raises the pull, called tension. Cut the stem under water while under tension, and scan again. Several conduits now hold air. Already there, or made by the cut?

scenes.visual: Hold the 'Before cut' and 'After cut' stem slices side by side on the right window with the question 'Already there, or made by the cut?' while a slow pulse highlights the newly air-filled conduits (schematic).

scenes.tts: Conduits full before and empty after were emptied by the cut. But did tension cause it? Rehydrate the plant until its water potential, a measure of that pull, is only slightly negative. Aim for about minus zero point two to minus zero point four megapascals. Rescan to check nothing refilled. Then compare matched cuts at low and high tension. Few new embolisms at low tension, many at high, point to tension.
scenes.caption: Conduits full before and empty after were emptied by the cut. But did tension cause it? Rehydrate the plant until its water potential, a measure of that pull, is only slightly negative. Aim for about -0.2 to -0.4 MPa. Rescan to check nothing refilled. Then compare matched cuts at low and high tension. Few new embolisms at low tension, many at high, point to tension.
scenes.visual: Same stage (schematic): the newly empty conduits flash 'Emptied by cut'. The stem rehydrates as a water-potential gauge beside the stage rises to '-0.2 to -0.4 MPa'; a re-scan shows the already-empty conduits still empty ('Nothing refilled'). Then two post-cut slices appear side by side, both labelled 'If' (schematic): 'Low tension' with few new bubbles, 'High tension' with many.
scenes.narration: Conduits full before and empty after were emptied by the cut. But did tension cause it? Rehydrate the plant until its water potential, a measure of that pull, is only slightly negative. Aim for about -0.2 to -0.4 MPa. Rescan to check nothing refilled. Then compare matched cuts at low and high tension. Few new embolisms at low tension, many at high, point to tension.

scenes.tts: Showing that cuts can create false embolisms does not prove intact stems never refill. That needs repeated scans of uncut stems. In insects, X-rays show tubes changing shape, not how much air moves. In 2015, Pendar, Kenny and Socha X-rayed beetle pupae while recording abdominal pumps and body-fluid pressure. Every tracheal collapse came with a pump. Yet in their recordings, sixty-three point seven percent of pumps came with no compression. So a pump alone did not show air being pushed.
scenes.caption: Showing that cuts can create false embolisms does not prove intact stems never refill. That needs repeated scans of uncut stems. In insects, X-rays show tubes changing shape, not how much air moves. In 2015, Pendar, Kenny and Socha X-rayed beetle pupae while recording abdominal pumps and body-fluid pressure. Every tracheal collapse came with a pump. Yet in their recordings, 63.7% of pumps came with no compression. So a pump alone did not show air being pushed.
scenes.visual: Same stage (schematic): the right window splits cleanly into two panels. Top: an uncut stem scanned repeatedly as a schematic clock turns ('Test refilling uncut'). Bottom: a beetle pupa on the stage, its abdomen pumping with a schematic pressure waveform; first a pump with tracheae collapsing ('Collapse = pump'), then pumps with tracheae still, and a bar showing '63.7% of pumps: no compression' (Pendar, Kenny and Socha, 2015).
scenes.narration: Showing that cuts can create false embolisms does not prove intact stems never refill. That needs repeated scans of uncut stems. In insects, X-rays show tubes changing shape, not how much air moves. In 2015, Pendar, Kenny and Socha X-rayed beetle pupae while recording abdominal pumps and body-fluid pressure. Every tracheal collapse came with a pump. Yet in their recordings, 63.7% of pumps came with no compression. So a pump alone did not show air being pushed.

scenes.tts: X-ray imaging unlocked three findings. In 2003, Mark Westneat and colleagues used synchrotron X-rays on live beetles, crickets and ants. Their tracheae compressed and expanded rhythmically, evidence that insects move air actively. In 2015, Torres-Ruiz and colleagues scanned stems at different tensions. Cutting under water while xylem was under tension itself created embolisms.
scenes.caption: X-ray imaging unlocked three findings. In 2003, Mark Westneat and colleagues used synchrotron X-rays on live beetles, crickets and ants. Their tracheae compressed and expanded rhythmically, evidence that insects move air actively. In 2015, Torres-Ruiz and colleagues scanned stems at different tensions. Cutting under water while xylem was under tension itself created embolisms.
scenes.visual: Same stage (schematic): first, a live beetle sits in the synchrotron beam as tracheae in its head and thorax squeeze and reopen in the right window ('Westneat et al., 2003'). Next, an intact plant stem replaces it and slices show water conduits turning air-filled after an underwater cut under tension ('Torres-Ruiz et al., 2015').
scenes.narration: X-ray imaging unlocked three findings. In 2003, Mark Westneat and colleagues used synchrotron X-rays on live beetles, crickets and ants. Their tracheae compressed and expanded rhythmically, evidence that insects move air actively. In 2015, Torres-Ruiz and colleagues scanned stems at different tensions. Cutting under water while xylem was under tension itself created embolisms.

scenes.tts: In 2018, Mathers and colleagues scanned leaf discs with micro C T. They measured the surface of mesophyll, the photosynthetic tissue, facing internal air spaces. Divide that surface by leaf area, and the units cancel. Barley gave twenty-one point three square millimetres per square millimetre: about twenty-one times its one-face area. Rice gave fifteen point five, about fifteen times. Each time, X-rays measured hidden structure without slicing it open.
scenes.caption: In 2018, Mathers and colleagues scanned leaf discs with microCT. They measured the surface of mesophyll, the photosynthetic tissue, facing internal air spaces. Divide that surface by leaf area, and the units cancel. Barley gave 21.3 mm² per mm²: about twenty-one times its one-face area. Rice gave 15.5, about fifteen times. Each time, X-rays measured hidden structure without slicing it open.
scenes.visual: Same stage (schematic): a small green leaf disc sits in the microCT beam, rebuilding a spongy 3D cross-section of internal air spaces and glowing mesophyll cell surfaces on the right. The formula 'mesophyll surface ÷ leaf area' appears with 'mm² / mm²' cancelling; bars grow to 21.3 for barley ('about 21 times') and 15.5 for rice ('about 15 times') (Mathers et al., 2018), then zoom out softly over the stage.

Each time, X-rays measured hidden structure without slicing it open.
